summary: Discusses how ICMP can be used to attack TCP connections, and describes widely implemented changes to TCP's handling of ICMP error messages that reduce these attacks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: ICMP error messages help report network problems, but a fake error can make TCP stop, slow down or send smaller packets. This RFC explains checks that make those attacks harder.

subtitle: How forged ICMP errors can disrupt TCP and how implementations limit their effect

tldr.problem: TCP implementations may act on ICMP error messages without checking whether they refer to data in the current connection. An off-path attacker who can guess the connection details can forge an error.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes checks on the TCP sequence number, port randomization and filtering, plus specific handling for reset, throughput-reduction and Path MTU Discovery attacks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents nonstandard countermeasures already used by some implementations. They can make TCP slower to react to genuine errors, but do not change the TCP standard.

today: RFC 5927 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents existing implementation countermeasures and does not change the TCP standard.

sections.title: Why ICMP Errors Can Affect TCP
sections.content:
ICMP reports network errors, and an ICMP error includes part of the packet that triggered it so the receiver can associate the error with a transport connection. The cited host requirements say TCP must act on an ICMP error passed up from IP, but the earlier specifications do not recommend validating the quoted packet.

An attacker can try to forge an error if they can guess the connection's source and destination addresses and ports. The RFC describes three possible results: reset a connection, reduce its throughput or make it perform poorly by changing its assumed path MTU. The attacks considered can be launched off path, without observing the TCP traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A network error message contains enough of an earlier packet to identify a TCP connection. If TCP trusts a forged message, it may disrupt a connection even when the attacker cannot see its traffic.

sections.title: General Checks on an Error Message
sections.content:
The available validation depends on how much of the original packet the ICMP message includes. For ICMPv4, the expected TCP information is the source and destination ports and the 32-bit sequence number. An implementation cannot recalculate a TCP or IPsec authentication value from that limited excerpt.

A widely implemented check accepts an ICMP error only when its quoted TCP sequence number lies in the range of data sent but not yet acknowledged: SND.UNA =< SEG.SEQ < SND.NXT. Randomizing outgoing port numbers makes the connection tuple harder to guess. Firewalls can also inspect the source address in the quoted packet and filter spoofed traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP can check whether an error refers to data it sent and has not yet heard back about. Random outgoing port numbers and filtering can make it harder to guess or forge the connection details.

sections.title: Forged Reset and Throughput Errors
sections.content:
A hard ICMP error can cause TCP to abort a connection. Many implementations instead treat hard errors received for connections in synchronized states as soft errors: they record the problem and continue retransmitting until the connection succeeds or times out. This improves resistance to forged resets but may delay response to a genuine failure.

A forged ICMPv4 Source Quench message can ask TCP to reduce its sending rate. The RFC notes that routers should not send Source Quench for congestion and TCP has its own congestion-control mechanisms. Many implementations therefore ignore Source Quench for TCP, despite the older host requirement to react to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Some TCP implementations keep an established connection open after a hard error instead of ending it immediately. They also ignore Source Quench messages, which could otherwise make TCP slow its sending rate.

sections.title: Protecting Path MTU Discovery
sections.content:
Path MTU Discovery uses ICMP messages to tell a sender that packets are too large for a link on the route. An attacker can forge a message claiming a very small next-hop MTU, leading TCP to send smaller packets and spend more processing on the same data. The RFC describes a two-stage check used by OpenBSD and NetBSD: honor plausible messages during initial discovery, but treat later reductions more cautiously.

After a path MTU has been established, a smaller claimed MTU is recorded as pending and acted on only after a segment times out the configured number of times. If the segment is acknowledged first, the pending error is cleared. The RFC says this can slow response to valid path changes; Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery avoids dependence on ICMP but may take longer to converge.
sections.plainLanguage: A forged message can tell a sender to use packets that are unnecessarily small. Once a connection has made progress, the sender can wait for evidence of loss before believing a new claim about packet size.

sections.title: Scope and Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The countermeasures described here target off-path attackers and do not prevent an attacker who can observe the connection. Sequence checks and delayed path-MTU updates may also cause TCP to respond less quickly to genuine network errors.

The RFC records widely implemented behavior but does not make that behavior part of standard TCP. It leaves other functionality problems with traditional Path MTU Discovery to separate work.
sections.plainLanguage: These checks make off-path attacks harder, but they cannot stop an attacker who can see the connection. They may also delay TCP's response to a real network problem.
